why_how.text: Traffic keeps right and passes on the left as the norm, and no pass may break the speed limit.
Motorcycles and cyclists are owed different kinds of space when you pass them.

scenario.text: Nina is behind a motorcycle riding near the left edge of a wide lane.

reasoning.text: A passed motorcycle keeps its whole lane width, and no car may share lane space with one however wide the lane.

result.text: Nina waits and passes by moving fully into the next lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a wide lane leaves room to slip past a motorcycle without changing lanes.

correction.text: No car may share lane space with a motorcycle, however wide the lane or one-sided the bike.

memory_support.text: Full lane for a motorcycle, safe berth for a bike.

prompt.text: You want to pass a cyclist riding ahead of you in your lane. How do you do it?

answer.text: Go left at a safe distance and hold it until the bicycle is clear.

rationale.text: Passed cyclists get sufficient room, with rear overtakes going left at a safe distance until the bicycle clears.

lines.text: Keep right, pass on the left.
Space for motorcycles and cyclists.

narration.text: This lesson starts the passing chapter with the ground rules. In New York, traffic keeps to the right, and passing goes on the left as the norm, with the right used only when it is necessary and safe. Any move you make to avoid a hazard stays as small as possible, and no pass ever allows you to break the speed limit. From there we look at the space you owe two kinds of road users when you pass them, motorcycles and cyclists, and then at two firm rules: the signal you give before a lane change, and the one stopped vehicle you may never pass.

lines.text: Traffic keeps right.
Pass on the left as the norm.
Never break the speed limit.

narration.text: The first rule is the norm for all passing. Traffic keeps right. When you pass, you go to the left, and you pass on the right only when that is necessary and safe. If you have to move to avoid a hazard, keep the move minimal. And no pass may break the speed limit. So the speed limit still applies for the whole pass, from the moment you pull out until you are back in the right lane. Keep right, pass left, keep any hazard move small, and stay within the limit. Hold these four parts together as the starting point for everything else in this chapter.

lines.text: The motorcycle keeps its whole lane.
No sharing, however wide the lane.
Even if the bike rides to one side.

narration.text: When you pass a motorcycle, the motorcycle keeps its whole lane width. No car may share lane space with a motorcycle, however wide the lane is, and however far to one side the bike is riding. So even if a motorcycle hugs one edge of a wide lane and seems to leave a gap, that gap is not yours. To pass, you move fully into the next lane, just as you would for a car. The rule is simple and absolute: one lane, one motorcycle. Keep it in mind next to the cyclist rule on the next slide, because the two work differently. This applies to every motorcycle you pass, however wide the lane.

lines.text: Give the cyclist sufficient room.
Overtake on the left.
Keep a safe distance until clear.

narration.text: Cyclists are owed room too, but the rule is worded differently. A passed cyclist gets sufficient room. When you overtake a bicycle from behind, you go to the left at a safe distance, and you keep that distance until you have cleared the bicycle. Notice that this is a judged space rather than a fixed lane. You decide what a safe distance is in the moment, and you hold it until the bicycle is behind you. You do not cut back in early, and you do not pass close. Room on the left, held until clear, is the whole cyclist rule in a few words.

lines.text: Motorcycle: a full untouched lane.
Cyclist: a safe berth on the left.
Absolute space versus judged space.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because motorcycles and bicycles are both two-wheelers, people assume the passing rule is the same. The manual sets them apart. A motorcycle demands a full untouched lane. A bicycle demands a safe berth on the left. One is absolute space and the other is judged space. So with a motorcycle, the question is never how much room you can leave inside its lane, because you may not share the lane at all. With a cyclist, the question is how much room is safe, and you keep that room until the bicycle is clear. Keep the two rules in separate boxes.

lines.text: Signal at least one hundred feet ahead.
Lamp or hand signals both count.
Never pass a car stopped at a crosswalk.

narration.text: Two more firm rules round out the basics. Before a lane change, signal at least one hundred feet ahead, using your signal lamps or hand signals. Either kind of signal meets the rule, as long as it comes at least one hundred feet before the move. And no driver may pass a vehicle that is stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian. So when a vehicle has stopped at a crosswalk for someone on foot, passing it is not allowed, whichever side you would pass on. The chapter's own review questions come back to this crosswalk-stop rule, so it is worth knowing cold.

lines.text: A cyclist is ahead in your lane.
How do you pass?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving behind a cyclist who is riding ahead of you in your lane, and you want to pass. How do you do it? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to overtake on the left at a safe distance, and to keep that safe distance until the bicycle has cleared. A cyclist gets sufficient room when you pass. If you answered that the cyclist gets a full untouched lane, that is the motorcycle rule. The motorcycle keeps its whole lane, while the cyclist gets a safe berth on the left that you judge and hold.

lines.text: Keep right; pass left within the limit.
Full lane for motorcycles.
Safe berth for cyclists; signal early.

narration.text: To close, traffic keeps right, passing goes left as the norm, right only when necessary and safe, hazard-avoiding moves stay minimal, and no pass may break the speed limit. A passed motorcycle keeps its whole lane width, and no car may share its lane. A passed cyclist gets sufficient room, with the overtake going left at a safe distance until the bicycle clears. Signal at least one hundred feet before a lane change, and never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian. Next we look at when a left pass is not allowed, and at the glances for passing.

why_how.text: A list of road conditions bars a left pass outright.
Passing and returning each use their own glance and signal script.

scenario.text: Omar is on a two-way road and sees an oncoming car well inside two hundred feet as he thinks about passing.

reasoning.text: Oncoming traffic inside two hundred feet is one of the conditions that bars a left pass.

result.text: Omar stays behind and waits for a clear stretch.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the same shoulder check to pull out and to return.

correction.text: Entry checks the left shoulder, while return checks the mirror plus the right shoulder and pavement.

memory_support.text: Left shoulder out, mirror and right shoulder back.

prompt.text: You are about to move into the left lane to pass. Which blind spot do you check over your shoulder?

answer.text: The left-shoulder blind spot that the mirrors miss.

rationale.text: Entry checks the left shoulder; the right shoulder belongs to the return.

lines.text: Conditions that bar a left pass.
The glance script for passing.

narration.text: This lesson answers two questions about the left pass. First, when is it not allowed at all? The manual lists a set of road conditions that rule it out, from solid yellow center lines to blind curves and nearby crossings. Second, when a pass is allowed, how do you carry it out safely? There is a set script of mirror checks, signals and shoulder glances for pulling out, and a different script for coming back to the right lane. We will work through the barring conditions, then the pass itself, and then the difference between the two glance scripts, which is easy to blur.

lines.text: Solid yellow center lines.
Gaps you cannot return from in time.
Oncoming traffic inside two hundred feet.

narration.text: Start with the conditions that bar a left pass. You may not pass across solid yellow center lines. You may not start a pass into a gap you cannot return from before a solid line farther ahead. You may not pass when oncoming traffic is inside two hundred feet. And you may not pass whenever oncoming traffic would suffer interference. These four are the first part of the list. If any one of them is present, the left pass is barred, and the next slide adds the places where your view is blocked. Solid yellow center lines, a gap with no way back before a far solid line, and oncoming traffic too close all lead to the same answer: no left pass.

lines.text: Blind curves and hillcrests.
One hundred feet of rail crossings.
One hundred feet of obstructed bridges, tunnels.

narration.text: The list continues with places where you cannot see. On two-way roads, you may not pass on blind curves or at hillcrests. You may not pass within one hundred feet of a two-way railroad crossing. And you may not pass within one hundred feet of an obstructed two-way bridge, tunnel or viaduct. Put these together with the line and traffic conditions from the last slide, and you have the full set of situations that rule out a left pass. The curves, crests, crossings and bridge rules all apply on two-way roads, where the left lane carries oncoming traffic.

lines.text: Mirror check, signal, left-shoulder check.
Enter the left lane.
Signal, mirror, right shoulder, return.

narration.text: When a pass is allowed, follow the script. First check your mirrors and signal. Then check over your left shoulder for the blind spot that the mirrors miss, and only then enter the left lane. To come back, signal again, and confirm two things: that you can see the front bumper of the car you passed in your rear-view mirror, and that the pavement is clear when you look over your right shoulder. Then return to the right lane. So the order out is mirrors, signal, left shoulder, and the order back is signal, passed bumper in the mirror, right shoulder and pavement.

lines.text: Going out: left shoulder.
Coming back: mirror and right shoulder.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because you glance over a shoulder both times, it is easy to think the same check covers pulling out and coming back. The manual describes two different glance scripts for two different moves. Entry checks the left shoulder. Return checks the mirror plus the right shoulder and the pavement. So before you move left, your shoulder glance goes left, to the blind spot the mirrors miss on that side. Before you move back right, you want the passed bumper in your rear-view mirror and a clear view over your right shoulder. Match each glance to its move.

lines.text: About to move left to pass.
Which shoulder do you check?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: the road ahead is clear, you have checked your mirrors and signaled, and you are about to move into the left lane to pass. Which blind spot do you check over your shoulder? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the left-shoulder blind spot, the one your mirrors miss on that side. If you answered the right shoulder, that check belongs to the return, when you confirm the passed bumper in your rear-view mirror and look over your right shoulder at the pavement before moving back. Going out and coming back each have their own glance.

lines.text: Seven conditions bar a left pass.
Left shoulder out, right shoulder back.

narration.text: To wrap up, a left pass is barred by solid yellow center lines, gaps you cannot return from before a far solid line, oncoming traffic inside two hundred feet, blind curves and hillcrests on two-way roads, within one hundred feet of two-way railroad crossings and of obstructed two-way bridges, tunnels and viaducts, and whenever oncoming traffic would suffer interference. When a pass is allowed, mirror-check, signal and check your left shoulder before moving out. To return, signal, confirm the passed bumper in the mirror and the pavement over your right shoulder. Next we cover passing on the right.

why_how.text: Right passing is a narrow exception with its own list of allowed cases.
Being passed has a set response too.

scenario.text: Kim is on a two-way road behind a car that has stopped to turn left.

reasoning.text: Right passes are allowed past a left-turning vehicle ahead, but never across shoulders or edge lines except by sign or officer.

result.text: Kim passes on the right within the travel lanes, staying off the shoulder.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a paved shoulder is fair game for passing a slow car on the right.

correction.text: Right passes never cross shoulders or edge lines except when a sign or an officer allows it.

memory_support.text: Left by default, right by exception, never the shoulder.

prompt.text: Another driver starts to pass you. What do you do?

answer.text: Slow slightly, hold the center of your lane, and resume speed once the other car is clear.

rationale.text: Passed drivers slow slightly and hold lane center; chronic right-side passing means moving right.

title.text: The right side and being passed

lines.text: When a right pass is allowed.
What to do when you are passed.

narration.text: This lesson looks at the other side of passing. The manual allows passing on the right only in a few set cases, and we will go through them for two-way roads, for one-way roads, and at intersections. Then we will line those cases up against the left-pass rules from the last lesson, because the two sides are built in opposite ways. Finally we turn the situation around and look at what you should do when another driver is passing you, including what it means when drivers keep passing you on the right. By the end you will know when the right side is open and when it is closed.

lines.text: Past a left-turning vehicle ahead.
Two-plus lanes each way, no bans.
Never across shoulders or edge lines.

narration.text: On a two-way road, a right pass is allowed in two situations. The first is when the vehicle ahead is turning left, or is about to. The second is when the road is marked for, or wide enough for, two or more lanes in each direction, with no prohibitions or obstructions. Either way, a right pass never crosses a shoulder or an edge line, unless a sign or an officer directs it. So a slow car ahead on an ordinary two-lane road is not by itself a reason to pass on the right. The case has to be one of these, and you stay within the travel lanes.

lines.text: One-way roads with two-plus lanes.
No bans or obstructions.
Check ahead and to the right.

narration.text: Right passes are also allowed on one-way roads that are marked for, or wide enough for, two or more lanes, again with no prohibitions or obstructions. When a right pass takes you through an intersection, add two checks. Look ahead for vehicles turning left, and look to your right for pedestrians, cyclists, skaters and moped riders. Both checks belong to every right pass through an intersection. With that, you have the full set of right-pass cases: a left-turner ahead, a wide two-way road, or a wide one-way road. On every one of these roads, the lanes must be free of prohibitions or obstructions.

lines.text: Left: the default, barred by conditions.
Right: the exception, allowed by cases.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People sometimes treat left and right passing as two equal options. The manual builds them in opposite ways. Left passing is the default, and it is barred by seven conditions, the lines, gaps, traffic, curves, crests, crossings and bridges from the last lesson. Right passing is the exception, and it is allowed by three cases, the left-turner ahead, the wide two-way road and the wide one-way road. So for a left pass you ask whether anything forbids it. For a right pass you ask whether something specifically allows it. If nothing allows it, the right side stays closed.

lines.text: Slow slightly; hold lane center.
Resume speed once clear.
Often passed on the right? Move right.

narration.text: Now turn it around. When another driver passes you, slow slightly, hold the center of your lane, and resume your speed once the other car is clear. Those three steps are the whole response to being passed. The manual adds one more point: if drivers keep passing you on the right side, that is a sign you should move right and free the left lane for them. So the response has two parts: slow slightly and hold lane center while the pass happens, and if you are passed on the right again and again, move right yourself. Slow slightly, hold center, resume: that is the order.

lines.text: Another car starts to pass you.
What do you do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving along a two-lane road and the car behind you pulls out and starts to pass. What do you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to slow slightly, hold the center of your lane, and resume your speed once the other car is clear. The manual asks passed drivers to slow slightly, not to speed up. And if you find that drivers keep passing you on the right side on a road with more than one lane your way, the manual says to move right and free the left lane rather than staying where you are.

lines.text: Right pass only in set cases.
Never across shoulders or edge lines.
Being passed: slow, hold center.

narration.text: To close, right passes are allowed only past a left-turning vehicle ahead, on two-way roads marked or wide enough for two-plus lanes each way, and on one-way roads marked or wide enough for two-plus lanes, without prohibitions or obstructions, and never across shoulders or edge lines except by sign or officer. At intersections, check ahead for left-turners and right for pedestrians, cyclists, skaters and moped riders. Left is the default and right the exception. When you are passed, slow slightly, hold lane center, then resume, and move right if you are often passed on the right.

why_how.text: Yellow and red flashers on a school bus mean different things, warning versus command.
Most bus deaths strike crossing children rather than bus occupants, so the care continues after the stop.

scenario.text: Rosa is on a divided highway when a school bus on the far side stops with red lights flashing.

reasoning.text: The stop applies on every New York roadway, including the far side of divided highways.

result.text: Rosa stops at least twenty feet back and waits until the bus moves or she is waved on.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a divided highway means you can keep going when a bus across the median stops with red lights flashing.

correction.text: Stopped drivers wait on every New York roadway, including the far side of divided highways.

memory_support.text: Yellow, get ready; red, stop both ways.

prompt.text: A school bus ahead stops with its red lights flashing. When may you move again?

answer.text: When the bus moves or the driver or an officer waves you on.

rationale.text: Red flashers halt both directions twenty feet back until release by the bus or a wave.

lines.text: Yellow flashers and red flashers.
Where, how far, and until when.

narration.text: This lesson is about school buses, one of the most serious parts of the passing chapter. The manual separates two signals on the bus: yellow flashers that warn a stop is coming, and red flashers that command traffic to stop. We will look at what each one asks of you, how far back to stop, where the rule applies, when you may move again, and what to watch for once the bus moves on. We will also cover which other vehicles get the same stops. The penalties come in the next lesson, after the rules for the stop itself. Let's begin with the yellow lights.

lines.text: Yellow roof flashers, front and back.
Slow down.
Be ready to stop.

narration.text: A school bus telegraphs its stops. Before it stops, it shows yellow roof flashers, front and back. Yellow flashers command slower speed and stop readiness. In other words, when you see yellow on a school bus, slow down and get ready to stop. The yellow flashers telegraph the stop from the roof, front and back. Yellow commands slower speed and readiness to stop. Keep that idea, yellow means get ready, because the next slide is about what red means, and the two are easy to blur. So yellow asks two things of you: slow down, and be ready to stop.

lines.text: Both directions stop.
At least twenty feet back.
School grounds and lots too.

narration.text: When a school bus is stopped with red lights flashing, traffic in both directions must stop. That applies everywhere, including on school grounds and in school parking lots. Stop at least twenty feet back from the bus. You can identify a school bus by its school-bus sign, its red roof lights, and its yellow-orange paint. The red flashers are a command, not a warning, and the rule covers drivers going the same way as the bus and drivers coming toward it. So when you see those red lights on a stopped bus, stop, keep your distance, and wait.

lines.text: Wait until the bus moves.
Or the driver or an officer waves you on.
Every roadway, even divided highways.

narration.text: Once you have stopped, stay stopped until the bus begins to roll, or until the bus driver or a police officer waves you on. That is the only release. The rule applies on every New York roadway, and that includes the far side of a divided highway. So even if a median separates you from the bus, you stop when its red lights are flashing. There is a related vehicle to know as well. Vehicles that carry people with disabilities and are built as school buses command identical stops, so treat them exactly the same way when their lights are flashing.

lines.text: Yellow: slow and get ready.
Red: stop both ways until released.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because both sets of lights flash, people treat them alike. The manual draws a clear line: yellow flashers only slow and ready the driver, while red flashers halt both directions twenty feet back until release. Yellow is a warning; red is a command. So if you see yellow, you slow and prepare, but you are not yet required to stop. If you see red on a stopped bus, you stop whichever direction you are going, stay at least twenty feet back, and wait for the bus to move or for a wave from the driver or an officer before you go on.

lines.text: Scan the roadside for children.
Creep past them.
Crossing children face the most risk.

narration.text: The care does not end when the bus moves. After the stop, scan the roadside for children and creep past them. The manual gives the reason directly: most school bus deaths strike children who are crossing, not the children riding inside the bus. That is why your attention stays on the road edges as you pull away. So after a bus stop, scan along the roadside for children and creep past them rather than pulling away at normal speed. The scan and the creep are the two steps the manual gives for the moment the bus moves on.

lines.text: A bus stops with red lights flashing.
When may you move again?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a school bus ahead of you stops and turns on its red flashing lights, and you stop at least twenty feet back. When may you move again? Work it out before reading on. The answer is when the bus begins to move, or when the bus driver or a police officer waves you on. Until then you stay stopped, in either direction, and on every New York roadway, including the far side of a divided highway. And once you do move, scan the roadside for children and creep past them, because crossing children face the greatest risk.

lines.text: Yellow: slow, be ready.
Red: both ways, twenty feet back.
Wait for release; watch for children.

narration.text: To close, a school bus shows yellow roof flashers front and back before it stops, which means slow down and be ready to stop. When it is stopped with red lights flashing, traffic in both directions stops at least twenty feet back, everywhere including school grounds and lots. A school bus is identified by its sign, its red roof lights and its yellow-orange paint. Wait until the bus moves or the driver or an officer waves you on, on every New York roadway. Then creep past watching for children. Disability-transport vehicles built as school buses get the same stops. Next come the penalties.

why_how.text: Passing a stopped school bus brings rising fines and, with repeats, license revocation.
Stop-arm cameras create a second track that bills vehicle owners.

scenario.text: A driver is convicted of passing a stopped school bus for the first time.

reasoning.text: Passing a stopped school bus fines two hundred fifty dollars first, rising for repeats.

result.text: The driver pays the first-offense fine, and three violations in three years would revoke the license.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a camera ticket and a driver conviction are the same penalty.

correction.text: Driver convictions fine up to one thousand with revocation on repeats, while camera tickets bill owners on a lower ladder.

memory_support.text: Conviction hits the driver; the camera bills the owner.

prompt.text: A driver is found guilty for the first time of passing a stopped school bus. How much is the fine?

rationale.text: That is the first rung of the driver-conviction ladder, which reaches one thousand for three violations in three years.

lines.text: Driver convictions.
Stop-arm camera tickets.

narration.text: This last lesson of the passing chapter covers what happens when a driver passes a stopped school bus. The manual describes two separate ways the offense is punished. The first is a conviction of the driver, with fines that climb for repeat violations and, at the top, revocation of the license. The second comes from a law that lets school districts and towns use stop-arm cameras to bill the owners of vehicles that pass stopped buses. We will look at each track, compare them side by side, and then finish with the chapter's own review topics as a checklist of the whole chapter.

lines.text: First conviction: two hundred fifty dollars.
Three in three years: up to one thousand.
And revocation for at least six months.

narration.text: Start with the driver conviction. Passing a stopped school bus brings a fine of two hundred fifty dollars for a first violation. The fines climb from there, up to one thousand dollars for three violations within three years. And three violations within three years also revoke the license for at least six months. So the conviction track has two parts: money that rises with each repeat, and, at the top, the loss of the license. This is the track that falls on the person who was driving, and it is the only one of the two tracks that names revocation.

lines.text: Stop-arm camera law, twenty-nineteen.
Districts and towns bill owners.
Two fifty, two seventy-five, three hundred.

narration.text: The second track comes from the twenty-nineteen stop-arm camera law. It lets school districts and towns bill the owners of vehicles that pass red-flashing stopped buses. The amounts climb too: two hundred fifty dollars for a first ticket, two hundred seventy-five dollars for a second within eighteen months, and three hundred dollars for a third and beyond within eighteen months. Notice who receives the bill: the owner of the vehicle. And notice the ladder: it rises in smaller steps than the conviction track and stops at three hundred dollars, with no revocation named on this track.

lines.text: Conviction: driver, fines to one thousand.
Revocation on repeats.
Camera: owner, a lower ladder.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because both tracks punish the same act, passing a stopped school bus, people blur them together. The manual calls them two punishment tracks for one offense. Driver convictions fine up to one thousand dollars, with license revocation on repeats. Camera tickets bill owners on a lower ladder. So if a question mentions revocation or a fine as high as one thousand dollars, it is about a conviction of the driver. If it mentions a bill to the owner from a stop-arm camera, with steps of two hundred fifty, two seventy-five and three hundred, it is the camera track.

lines.text: A first conviction for passing a bus.
What is the fine?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted for the first time of passing a stopped school bus. What is the fine? Work it out before reading on. The answer is two hundred fifty dollars. That is the first rung of the conviction ladder, which climbs up to one thousand dollars for three violations within three years, along with revocation of at least six months. If you answered two hundred seventy-five dollars, that is the second camera ticket within eighteen months, which is billed to the owner on the separate camera track rather than charged to the convicted driver.

lines.text: Penalties fall on drivers and owners.
Review topics recap the chapter.

narration.text: To wrap up, a conviction for passing a stopped school bus fines two hundred fifty dollars first, up to one thousand for three violations in three years, with three in three years revoking the license for at least six months. The stop-arm camera law lets districts and towns bill owners two hundred fifty, then two seventy-five, then three hundred within eighteen months. The chapter closes with review questions on passing side, pre-pass checks, the mirror check before returning, right-pass conditions, the crosswalk-stop rule, being passed, and bus warning lights. Those topics are the lessons you have just worked through.
